title: Fewer Curry Houses, Better Curry: How Britain's Indian Restaurant Scene Is Trading Quantity for Quality
excerpt: The number of South Asian restaurants in the UK has dropped from 12,000 to 8,000 in a decade — but the industry says the real story is one of evolution, not decline.
body:
In 2016, there were roughly 12,000 South Asian restaurants across the United Kingdom. Today, that number stands at just over 8,000. On paper, the decline looks alarming — a third of the country's curry houses have vanished in barely a decade. But at the inaugural Global Edition of the Restaurant India Conference, held in London on May 28, some of the industry's most prominent voices argued that the numbers tell the wrong story entirely.

"The story today is about quality, not quantity," declared Samson Sohail, Head of Global Sales at Cobra Beer Molson Coors, during a panel moderated by Sanjay Anand, the veteran restaurateur behind Madhu's, which has anchored London's Indian dining scene for nearly four decades.

## The Old Guard Falls, the New Guard Rises

The explanation is straightforward: during the 1970s and 1980s boom, thousands of curry houses opened across Britain to serve a market that was largely unfamiliar with Indian food. Many operated on thin margins, limited menus, and formulaic formats — tikka masala, poppadoms, a Cobra, and the bill. That model sustained a generation but left the industry vulnerable when costs rose, labour tightened, and consumers grew more adventurous.

The restaurants that have closed were overwhelmingly of this older type. What has replaced them — or emerged alongside the survivors — is a fundamentally different proposition. Michelin-starred establishments like Benares, award-winning brands like Jamavar and Tresind, and chef-led independents like Kahani and Kutir are redefining what Indian food means in Britain.

The 2026 Global Indian Restaurant Awards, presented at the London conference, underscored the shift. Sanjeev Kapoor was named Global Indian Chef of the Year. The Cinnamon Club's Cinnamon Collection took Global Indian Restaurant of the Year. Atul Kochhar received the Culinary Excellence Award. Cafe Spice Namaste won the Culinary Heritage Award — recognition of both its longevity and its commitment to authentic regional cooking.

## "If You Want the World Stage, You Have to Be in London"

For Anjan Chatterjee, founder of Speciality Restaurants — a portfolio of nearly 150 outlets spanning India, the Gulf, and the United Kingdom — London remains the ultimate proving ground.

"London is the Mecca of hospitality, and I always knew we would come here one day," Chatterjee told the conference. Rather than exporting Mainland China, one of India's most successful restaurant brands, his group chose to bring an evolved version of Oh! Calcutta to the UK market, showcasing Bengali cuisine to an international audience.

But expansion has hit an unexpected wall: talent. Increasingly restrictive UK work-permit regulations have made it difficult to bring experienced chefs from India. "To deliver authentic cuisine, you need people who understand the food, the ingredients, and the culture of the organisation," Chatterjee said. Plans for a second London location have been postponed — not for lack of demand, but because finding the right kitchen talent has become the industry's single biggest challenge.

## The Michelin Question

Chef Sameer Taneja, Executive Chef at Benares and a Michelin-starred practitioner, offered a personal lens on the transformation. His early career focused on European cuisine before a pivotal decision to dedicate himself fully to Indian food.

"Everything changed the day I decided to cook my mother cuisine, Indian food," he said. At Benares, he champions a team-first philosophy: "A Michelin star is not an individual's identity. It belongs to the team that earns it together."

The comment touches on a broader truth. Indian cuisine's path to fine-dining recognition in the West has been slower than French, Japanese, or Scandinavian cooking — despite being, as Sanjay Anand argued, "among the most complex and technically demanding in the world." The tide is turning. Three Indian restaurants now hold Michelin stars in the US alone, and the London scene boasts several more.

## What This Means for NRIs

For diaspora Indians in Britain — and increasingly in America, where the restaurant landscape is following a similar arc — the quality revolution carries emotional weight. The neighbourhood curry house was often the first and only place where homesick NRIs could taste something familiar. Its decline can feel like a loss.

But the restaurants rising in its place are doing something the old model never could: they are making Indian food aspirational. The new generation of restaurateurs is proving that biryani can share a dining room with a Michelin star, that a dosa can be plated with the precision of a French terrine, and that Indian hospitality — warm, generous, deeply personal — is itself a competitive advantage on the global stage.

## What's Next

Kate Alexander, Head of Food and Commercial Channels at Nestle Professional UK and Ireland, pointed to a growing consumer demand for authentic regional Indian flavours, not just the familiar North Indian canon. "Demand for broader Asian flavours is accelerating, driven by consumers seeking greater authenticity and regional specificity," she said.

For an industry that built its British presence on a narrow menu, the future lies in breadth: Bengali, Keralan, Chettinad, Rajasthani, Konkani. The curry house may be dying. But Indian food in Britain has never been more alive.
